The presence of either a positive or negative electric charge produces an <color=#3366CC>electric field</color>. The motion of electric charge

carriers is an <color=#3366CC>electric current</color> and produces a <color=#3366CC>magnetic field</color>. In most applications, <color=#3366CC>Coulomb's law</color> determines the <color=#3366CC>force</color>
acting on an electrically charged <color=#3366CC>particle</color>. <color=#3366CC>Electric potential</color> is the <color=#3366CC>work</color> done to move an electric charge from one
position to another within an electric field, typically measured in <color=#3366CC>volts</color>.
Electricity plays a central role in many modern technologies, serving in <color=#3366CC>electric power</color> where electric current is used to

energise equipment, and in <color=#3366CC>electronics</color> dealing with <color=#3366CC>electrical circuits</color> involving <color=#3366CC>active components</color> such as <color=#3366CC>vacuum</color>
<color=#3366CC>tubes</color>, <color=#3366CC>transistors</color>, <color=#3366CC>diodes</color> and <color=#3366CC>integrated circuits</color>, and associated passive interconnection technologies.
The study of electrical phenomena dates back to antiquity, with theoretical understanding progressing slowly until the
17th and 18th centuries. The development of the theory of electromagnetism in the 19th century marked significant
progress, leading to electricity's industrial and residential application by <color=#3366CC>electrical engineers</color> by the century's end. This
rapid expansion in electrical technology at the time was the driving force behind the <color=#3366CC>Second Industrial Revolution</color>, with
electricity's versatility driving transformations in both industry and society. Electricity is integral to applications spanning

<color=#3366CC>transport</color>, <color=#3366CC>heating/cooling</color>, <color=#3366CC>lighting</color>, <color=#3366CC>communications</color>, and <color=#3366CC>computation</color>, making it the foundation of modern industrial
society.
History
Long before any knowledge of electricity existed, people were aware of shocks from electric fish. <color=#3366CC>Ancient Egyptian</color> texts
dating from 2750 BCE described them as the "protectors" of all other fish. Electric fish were again reported millennia

later by <color=#3366CC>ancient Greek</color>, <color=#3366CC>Roman</color> and <color=#3366CC>Arab naturalists</color> and <color=#3366CC>physicians</color>. Several ancient writers, such as <color=#3366CC>Pliny the Elder</color>
and Scribonius Largus, attested to the numbing effect of electric shocks delivered by electric catfish and <color=#3366CC>electric rays</color>,
and knew that such shocks could travel along conducting objects. Patients with ailments such as <color=#3366CC>gout</color> or <color=#3366CC>headache</color>
were directed to touch electric fish in the hope that the powerful jolt might cure them.
Ancient cultures around the <color=#3366CC>Mediterranean</color> knew that certain objects, such as rods of <color=#3366CC>amber</color>, could be rubbed with cat's
fur to attract light objects like feathers. <color=#3366CC>Thales of Miletus</color> made a series of observations on <color=#3366CC>static electricity</color> around 600
BCE, from which he believed that friction rendered amber <color=#3366CC>magnetic</color>, in contrast to minerals such as <color=#3366CC>magnetite</color>, which
needed no rubbing. Thales was incorrect in believing the attraction was due to a magnetic effect, but later science
would prove a link between magnetism and electricity.
Electricity would remain little more than an intellectual curiosity for millennia until 1600, when the English scientist
<color=#3366CC>William Gilbert</color> wrote De Magnete, in which he made a careful study of electricity and magnetism, distinguishing the
lodestone effect from static electricity produced by rubbing amber. He coined the <color=#3366CC>Neo-Latin</color> word electricus ("of amber"
or "like amber", from, elektron, the <color=#3366CC>Greek</color> word for "amber") to refer to the property of attracting small objects after
being rubbed. This association gave rise to the English words "electric" and "electricity", which made their first
appearance in print in <color=#3366CC>Thomas Browne</color>'s Pseudodoxia Epidemica of 1646. <color=#3366CC>Isaac Newton</color> made early investigations into
electricity, with an idea of his written down in his book <color=#3366CC>Opticks</color> arguably the beginning of the <color=#3366CC>field theory</color> of the electric
force.
Further work was conducted in the 17th and early 18th centuries by <color=#3366CC>Otto von Guericke</color>, <color=#3366CC>Robert Boyle</color>, <color=#3366CC>Stephen Gray</color>
and C. F. du Fay. Later in the 18th century, <color=#3366CC>Benjamin Franklin</color> conducted extensive research in electricity, selling his
possessions to fund his work. In June 1752 he is reputed to have attached a metal key to the bottom of a dampened
kite string and flown the kite in a storm-threatened sky. A succession of sparks jumping from the key to the back of his
hand showed that <color=#3366CC>lightning</color> was indeed electrical in nature. He also explained the apparently paradoxical behaviour of
the <color=#3366CC>Leyden jar</color> as a device for storing large amounts of electrical charge in terms of electricity consisting of both positive
and negative charges.
In 1775, Hugh Williamson reported a series of experiments to the Royal Society on the shocks delivered by the <color=#3366CC>electric</color>
<color=#3366CC>eel</color>; that same year the surgeon and anatomist <color=#3366CC>John Hunter</color> described the structure of the fish's electric organs. In
1791, <color=#3366CC>Luigi Galvani</color> published his discovery of bioelectromagnetics, demonstrating that electricity was the medium by
which <color=#3366CC>neurons</color> passed signals to the muscles. <color=#3366CC>Alessandro Volta</color>'s battery, or voltaic pile, of 1800, made from alternating
layers of zinc and copper, provided scientists with a more reliable source of electrical energy than the electrostatic
machines previously used. The recognition of <color=#3366CC>electromagnetism</color>, the unity of electric and magnetic phenomena, is due

to <color=#3366CC>Hans Christian Ørsted</color> and <color=#3366CC>André-Marie Ampère</color> in 1819–1820. <color=#3366CC>Michael Faraday</color> invented the <color=#3366CC>electric motor</color> in 1821,
and <color=#3366CC>Georg Ohm</color> mathematically analysed the electrical circuit in 1827. Electricity and magnetism (and light) were
definitively linked by <color=#3366CC>James Clerk Maxwell</color>, in particular in his "On Physical Lines of Force" in 1861 and 1862.
While the early 19th century had seen rapid progress in electrical science, the late 19th century would see the greatest
progress in <color=#3366CC>electrical engineering</color>. Through such people as <color=#3366CC>Alexander Graham Bell</color>, Ottó Bláthy, <color=#3366CC>Thomas Edison</color>,
Galileo Ferraris, <color=#3366CC>Oliver Heaviside</color>, Ányos Jedlik, <color=#3366CC>William Thomson, 1st Baron Kelvin</color>, <color=#3366CC>Charles Algernon Parsons</color>,

<color=#3366CC>Werner von Siemens</color>, Joseph Swan, <color=#3366CC>Reginald Fessenden</color>, <color=#3366CC>Nikola Tesla</color> and <color=#3366CC>George Westinghouse</color>, electricity turned
from a scientific curiosity into an essential tool for modern life.
In 1887, <color=#3366CC>Heinrich Hertz</color> discovered that <color=#3366CC>electrodes</color> illuminated with ultraviolet light create electric sparks more easily. In
1905, <color=#3366CC>Albert Einstein</color> published a paper that explained experimental data from the <color=#3366CC>photoelectric effect</color> as being the
result of light energy being carried in discrete quantized packets, energising electrons. This discovery led to the
<color=#3366CC>quantum</color> revolution. Einstein was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1921 for "his discovery of the law of the
photoelectric effect". The photoelectric effect is also employed in photocells such as can be found in <color=#3366CC>solar panels</color>.
The first solid-state device was the "cat's-whisker detector" first used in the 1900s in radio receivers. A whisker-like wire
is placed lightly in contact with a solid crystal (such as a <color=#3366CC>germanium</color> crystal) to detect a <color=#3366CC>radio</color> signal by the contact
junction effect. In a solid-state component, the <color=#3366CC>current</color> is confined to solid elements and compounds engineered
specifically to switch and amplify it. Current flow can be understood in two forms: as negatively charged <color=#3366CC>electrons</color>, and
as positively charged electron deficiencies called <color=#3366CC>holes</color>. These charges and holes are understood in terms of quantum
physics. The building material is most often a crystalline <color=#3366CC>semiconductor</color>.
Solid-state electronics came into its own with the emergence of <color=#3366CC>transistor</color> technology. The first working transistor, a

<color=#3366CC>germanium</color>-based point-contact transistor, was invented by <color=#3366CC>John Bardeen</color> and <color=#3366CC>Walter Houser Brattain</color> at <color=#3366CC>Bell Labs</color> in
1947, followed by the <color=#3366CC>bipolar junction transistor</color> in 1948.
Concepts
Electric charge
By modern convention, the charge carried by <color=#3366CC>electrons</color> is defined as negative, and that by <color=#3366CC>protons</color> is positive. Before
these particles were discovered, <color=#3366CC>Benjamin Franklin</color> had defined a positive charge as being the charge acquired by a
glass rod when it is rubbed with a silk cloth. A proton by definition carries a charge of exactly 1.602176634×10^-19
coulombs. This value is also defined as the <color=#3366CC>elementary charge</color>. No object can have a charge smaller than the
elementary charge, and any amount of charge an object may carry is a multiple of the elementary charge. An electron
has an equal negative charge, i.e. -1.602176634×10^-19 coulombs. Charge is possessed not just by <color=#3366CC>matter</color>, but also
by <color=#3366CC>antimatter</color>, each <color=#3366CC>antiparticle</color> bearing an equal and opposite charge to its corresponding particle.
The presence of charge gives rise to an electrostatic force: charges exert a <color=#3366CC>force</color> on each other, an effect that was
known, though not understood, in antiquity. A lightweight ball suspended by a fine thread can be charged by touching it
with a glass rod that has itself been charged by rubbing with a cloth. If a similar ball is charged by the same glass rod, it
is found to repel the first: the charge acts to force the two balls apart. Two balls that are charged with a rubbed amber
rod also repel each other. However, if one ball is charged by the glass rod, and the other by an amber rod, the two balls
are found to attract each other. These phenomena were investigated in the late eighteenth century by <color=#3366CC>Charles-Augustin</color>
<color=#3366CC>de Coulomb</color>, who deduced that charge manifests itself in two opposing forms. This discovery led to the well-known
axiom: like-charged objects repel and opposite-charged objects attract.
The force acts on the charged particles themselves, hence charge has a tendency to spread itself as evenly as
possible over a conducting surface. The magnitude of the electromagnetic force, whether attractive or repulsive, is
given by <color=#3366CC>Coulomb's law</color>, which relates the force to the product of the charges and has an <color=#3366CC>inverse-square</color> relation to the
distance between them. The electromagnetic force is very strong, second only in strength to the <color=#3366CC>strong interaction</color>, but
unlike that force it operates over all distances. In comparison with the much weaker <color=#3366CC>gravitational force</color>, the
electromagnetic force pushing two electrons apart is 1042 times that of the <color=#3366CC>gravitational</color> attraction pulling them
together.
Charge originates from certain types of <color=#3366CC>subatomic particles</color>, the most familiar carriers of which are the <color=#3366CC>electron</color> and
<color=#3366CC>proton</color>. Electric charge gives rise to and interacts with the <color=#3366CC>electromagnetic force</color>, one of the four <color=#3366CC>fundamental forces</color> of
nature. Experiment has shown charge to be a <color=#3366CC>conserved quantity</color>, that is, the net charge within an electrically isolated
system will always remain constant regardless of any changes taking place within that system. Within the system,
charge may be transferred between bodies, either by direct contact or by passing along a conducting material, such as
a wire. The informal term <color=#3366CC>static electricity</color> refers to the net presence (or 'imbalance') of charge on a body, usually
caused when dissimilar materials are rubbed together, transferring charge from one to the other.
Charge can be measured by a number of means, an early instrument being the gold-leaf electroscope, which although
still in use for classroom demonstrations, has been superseded by the electronic electrometer.
Electric current
The movement of electric charge is known as an <color=#3366CC>electric current</color>, the intensity of which is usually measured in <color=#3366CC>amperes</color>.
Current can consist of any moving charged particles; most commonly these are electrons, but any charge in motion
constitutes a current. Electric current can flow through some things, <color=#3366CC>electrical conductors</color>, but will not flow through an
<color=#3366CC>electrical insulator</color>.
By historical convention, a positive current is defined as having the same direction of flow as any positive charge it
contains, or to flow from the most positive part of a circuit to the most negative part. Current defined in this manner is
called <color=#3366CC>conventional current</color>. The motion of negatively charged electrons around an <color=#3366CC>electric circuit</color>, one of the most
familiar forms of current, is thus deemed positive in the opposite direction to that of the electrons. However, depending
on the conditions, an electric current can consist of a flow of charged particles in either direction or even in both
directions at once. The positive-to-negative convention is widely used to simplify this situation.
The process by which electric current passes through a material is termed <color=#3366CC>electrical conduction</color>, and its nature varies
with that of the charged particles and the material through which they are travelling. Examples of electric currents
include metallic conduction, where electrons flow through a <color=#3366CC>conductor</color> such as metal, and <color=#3366CC>electrolysis</color>, where <color=#3366CC>ions</color>
(charged <color=#3366CC>atoms</color>) flow through liquids, or through <color=#3366CC>plasmas</color> such as electrical sparks. While the particles themselves can
move quite slowly, sometimes with an average drift velocity only fractions of a millimetre per second, the <color=#3366CC>electric field</color>
that drives them itself propagates at close to the <color=#3366CC>speed of light</color>, enabling electrical signals to pass rapidly along wires.
Current causes several observable effects, which historically were the means of recognising its presence. That water
could be decomposed by the current from a voltaic pile was discovered by Nicholson and Carlisle in 1800, a process
now known as <color=#3366CC>electrolysis</color>. Their work was greatly expanded upon by <color=#3366CC>Michael Faraday</color> in 1833. Current through a
<color=#3366CC>resistance</color> causes localised heating, an effect <color=#3366CC>James Prescott Joule</color> studied mathematically in 1840. One of the most
important discoveries relating to current was made accidentally by <color=#3366CC>Hans Christian Ørsted</color> in 1820, when, while
preparing a lecture, he witnessed the current in a wire disturbing the needle of a magnetic compass. He had discovered
<color=#3366CC>electromagnetism</color>, a fundamental interaction between electricity and magnetics. The level of electromagnetic emissions
generated by electric arcing is high enough to produce electromagnetic interference, which can be detrimental to the
workings of adjacent equipment.
In engineering or household applications, current is often described as being either <color=#3366CC>direct current</color> (DC) or <color=#3366CC>alternating</color>
<color=#3366CC>current</color> (AC). These terms refer to how the current varies in time. Direct current, as produced by example from a <color=#3366CC>battery</color>
and required by most <color=#3366CC>electronic</color> devices, is a unidirectional flow from the positive part of a circuit to the negative. If, as
is most common, this flow is carried by electrons, they will be travelling in the opposite direction. Alternating current is
any current that reverses direction repeatedly; almost always this takes the form of a sine wave. Alternating current
thus pulses back and forth within a conductor without the charge moving any net distance over time. The
time-averaged value of an alternating current is zero, but it delivers energy in first one direction, and then the reverse.
Alternating current is affected by electrical properties that are not observed under <color=#3366CC>steady state</color> direct current, such as
<color=#3366CC>inductance</color> and <color=#3366CC>capacitance</color>. These properties however can become important when circuitry is subjected to transients,
such as when first energised.
Electric field
The concept of the electric <color=#3366CC>field</color> was introduced by <color=#3366CC>Michael Faraday</color>. An electric field is created by a charged body in
the space that surrounds it, and results in a force exerted on any other charges placed within the field. The electric field
acts between two charges in a similar manner to the way that the gravitational field acts between two <color=#3366CC>masses</color>, and like
it, extends towards infinity and shows an inverse square relationship with distance. However, there is an important
difference. Gravity always acts in attraction, drawing two masses together, while the electric field can result in either
attraction or repulsion. Since large bodies such as planets generally carry no net charge, the electric field at a distance
is usually zero. Thus gravity is the dominant force at distance in the universe, despite being much weaker.
An electric field generally varies in space, and its strength at any one point is defined as the force (per unit charge) that
would be felt by a stationary, negligible charge if placed at that point. The conceptual charge, termed a '<color=#3366CC>test charge</color>',
must be vanishingly small to prevent its own electric field disturbing the main field and must also be stationary to
prevent the effect of <color=#3366CC>magnetic fields</color>. As the electric field is defined in terms of <color=#3366CC>force</color>, and force is a <color=#3366CC>vector</color>, having both
<color=#3366CC>magnitude</color> and <color=#3366CC>direction</color>, it follows that an electric field is a <color=#3366CC>vector field</color>.
The study of electric fields created by stationary charges is called <color=#3366CC>electrostatics</color>. The field may be visualised by a set of
imaginary lines whose direction at any point is the same as that of the field. This concept was introduced by Faraday,
whose term 'lines of force' still sometimes sees use. The field lines are the paths that a point positive charge would
seek to make as it was forced to move within the field; they are however an imaginary concept with no physical
existence, and the field permeates all the intervening space between the lines. Field lines emanating from stationary
charges have several key properties: first, they originate at positive charges and terminate at negative charges;
second, they must enter any good conductor at right angles, and third, they may never cross nor close in on
themselves.
A hollow conducting body carries all its charge on its outer surface. The field is therefore 0 at all places inside the body.
This is the operating principle of the <color=#3366CC>Faraday cage</color>, a conducting metal shell that isolates its interior from outside
electrical effects.
The principles of electrostatics are important when designing items of high-voltage equipment. There is a finite limit to
the electric field strength that may be withstood by any medium. Beyond this point, electrical breakdown occurs and an
electric arc causes flashover between the charged parts. Air, for example, tends to arc across small gaps at electric
field strengths which exceed 30 kV per centimetre. Over larger gaps, its breakdown strength is weaker, perhaps 1 kV
per centimetre. The most visible natural occurrence of this is <color=#3366CC>lightning</color>, caused when charge becomes separated in the
clouds by rising columns of air, and raises the electric field in the air to greater than it can withstand. The voltage of a
large lightning cloud may be as high as 100 MV and have discharge energies as great as 250 kWh.
The field strength is greatly affected by nearby conducting objects, and it is particularly intense when it is forced to
curve around sharply pointed objects. This principle is exploited in the <color=#3366CC>lightning conductor</color>, the sharp spike of which
acts to encourage the lightning strike to develop there, rather than to the building it serves to protect.
Electric potential
The concept of electric potential is closely linked to that of the electric field. A small charge placed within an electric
field experiences a force, and to have brought that charge to that point against the force requires <color=#3366CC>work</color>. The electric
potential at any point is defined as the energy required to bring a unit test charge from an infinite distance slowly to that
point. It is usually measured in <color=#3366CC>volts</color>, and one volt is the potential for which one <color=#3366CC>joule</color> of work must be expended to bring
a charge of one <color=#3366CC>coulomb</color> from infinity. This definition of potential, while formal, has little practical application, and a
more useful concept is that of <color=#3366CC>electric potential difference</color>, and is the energy required to move a unit charge between
two specified points. The electric field is <color=#3366CC>conservative</color>, which means that the path taken by the test charge is irrelevant:
all paths between two specified points expend the same energy, and thus a unique value for potential difference may
be stated. The volt is so strongly identified as the unit of choice for measurement and description of electric potential
difference that the term <color=#3366CC>voltage</color> sees greater everyday usage.
For practical purposes, defining a common reference point to which potentials may be expressed and compared is
useful. While this could be at infinity, a much more useful reference is the <color=#3366CC>Earth</color> itself, which is assumed to be at the
same potential everywhere. This reference point naturally takes the name <color=#3366CC>earth</color> or ground. Earth is assumed to be an
infinite source of equal amounts of positive and negative charge and is therefore electrically uncharged—and
unchargeable.
Electric potential is a <color=#3366CC>scalar quantity</color>. That is, it has only magnitude and not direction. It may be viewed as analogous to
<color=#3366CC>height</color>: just as a released object will fall through a difference in heights caused by a gravitational field, so a charge will
'fall' across the voltage caused by an electric field. As relief maps show <color=#3366CC>contour lines</color> marking points of equal height, a
set of lines marking points of equal potential (known as <color=#3366CC>equipotentials</color>) may be drawn around an electrostatically
charged object. The equipotentials cross all lines of force at right angles. They must also lie parallel to a <color=#3366CC>conductor</color>'s
surface, since otherwise there would be a force along the surface of the conductor that would move the charge carriers
to even the potential across the surface.
The electric field was formally defined as the force exerted per unit charge, but the concept of potential allows for a
more useful and equivalent definition: the electric field is the local <color=#3366CC>gradient</color> of the electric potential. Usually expressed in
volts per metre, the vector direction of the field is the line of greatest slope of potential, and where the equipotentials lie
closest together.
Electromagnets
Ørsted's discovery in 1821 that a <color=#3366CC>magnetic field</color> existed around all sides of a wire carrying an electric current indicated
that there was a direct relationship between electricity and magnetism. Moreover, the interaction seemed different from
gravitational and electrostatic forces, the two forces of nature then known. The force on the compass needle did not
direct it to or away from the current-carrying wire, but acted at right angles to it. Ørsted's words were that "the electric
conflict acts in a revolving manner." The force also depended on the direction of the current, for if the flow was
reversed, then the force did too.
Ørsted did not fully understand his discovery, but he observed the effect was reciprocal: a current exerts a force on a
magnet, and a magnetic field exerts a force on a current. The phenomenon was further investigated by <color=#3366CC>Ampère</color>, who
discovered that two parallel current-carrying wires exerted a force upon each other: two wires conducting currents in
the same direction are attracted to each other, while wires containing currents in opposite directions are forced apart.
The interaction is mediated by the magnetic field each current produces and forms the basis for the international
<color=#3366CC>definition of the ampere</color>.
This relationship between magnetic fields and currents is extremely important, for it led to Michael Faraday's invention
of the <color=#3366CC>electric motor</color> in 1821. Faraday's homopolar motor consisted of a <color=#3366CC>permanent magnet</color> sitting in a pool of <color=#3366CC>mercury</color>.
A current was allowed through a wire suspended from a pivot above the magnet and dipped into the mercury. The
magnet exerted a tangential force on the wire, making it circle around the magnet for as long as the current was
maintained.
Experimentation by Faraday in 1831 revealed that a wire moving perpendicular to a magnetic field developed a
potential difference between its ends. Further analysis of this process, known as <color=#3366CC>electromagnetic induction</color>, enabled
him to state the principle, now known as <color=#3366CC>Faraday's law of induction</color>, that the potential difference induced in a closed
circuit is proportional to the rate of change of <color=#3366CC>magnetic flux</color> through the loop. Exploitation of this discovery enabled him
to invent the first <color=#3366CC>electrical generator</color> in 1831, in which he converted the mechanical energy of a rotating copper disc to
electrical energy. Faraday's disc was inefficient and of no use as a practical generator, but it showed the possibility of
generating electric power using magnetism, a possibility that would be taken up by those that followed on from his
work.
Electric circuits
An electric circuit is an interconnection of electric components such that electric charge is made to flow along a closed
path (a circuit), usually to perform some useful task.
The components in an electric circuit can take many forms, which can include elements such as <color=#3366CC>resistors</color>, <color=#3366CC>capacitors</color>,

<color=#3366CC>switches</color>, <color=#3366CC>transformers</color> and <color=#3366CC>electronics</color>. <color=#3366CC>Electronic circuits</color> contain <color=#3366CC>active components</color>, usually <color=#3366CC>semiconductors</color>, and
typically exhibit <color=#3366CC>non-linear</color> behaviour, requiring complex analysis. The simplest electric components are those that are
termed passive and linear: while they may temporarily store energy, they contain no sources of it, and exhibit linear
responses to stimuli.
The <color=#3366CC>resistor</color> is perhaps the simplest of passive circuit elements: as its name suggests, it <color=#3366CC>resists</color> the current through it,
dissipating its energy as heat. The resistance is a consequence of the motion of charge through a conductor: in metals,
for example, resistance is primarily due to collisions between electrons and ions. <color=#3366CC>Ohm's law</color> is a basic law of circuit
theory, stating that the current passing through a resistance is directly proportional to the potential difference across it.
The resistance of most materials is relatively constant over a range of temperatures and currents; materials under
these conditions are known as 'ohmic'. The <color=#3366CC>ohm</color>, the unit of resistance, was named in honour of <color=#3366CC>Georg Ohm</color>, and is
symbolised by the Greek letter. 1 is the resistance that will produce a potential difference of one volt in response to a
current of one amp.
The <color=#3366CC>capacitor</color> is a development of the Leyden jar and is a device that can store charge, and thereby storing electrical
energy in the resulting field. It consists of two conducting plates separated by a thin <color=#3366CC>insulating</color> <color=#3366CC>dielectric</color> layer; in
practice, thin metal foils are coiled together, increasing the surface area per unit volume and therefore the <color=#3366CC>capacitance</color>.
The unit of capacitance is the <color=#3366CC>farad</color>, named after <color=#3366CC>Michael Faraday</color>, and given the symbol F: one farad is the
capacitance that develops a potential difference of one volt when it stores a charge of one coulomb. A capacitor
connected to a voltage supply initially causes a current as it accumulates charge; this current will however decay in
time as the capacitor fills, eventually falling to zero. A capacitor will therefore not permit a <color=#3366CC>steady state</color> current, but
instead blocks it.
The <color=#3366CC>inductor</color> is a conductor, usually a coil of wire, that stores energy in a magnetic field in response to the current
through it. When the current changes, the magnetic field does too, <color=#3366CC>inducing</color> a voltage between the ends of the
conductor. The induced voltage is proportional to the <color=#3366CC>time rate of change</color> of the current. The constant of proportionality
is termed the <color=#3366CC>inductance</color>. The unit of inductance is the <color=#3366CC>henry</color>, named after <color=#3366CC>Joseph Henry</color>, a contemporary of Faraday.
One henry is the inductance that will induce a potential difference of one volt if the current through it changes at a rate
of one ampere per second. The inductor's behaviour is in some regards converse to that of the capacitor: it will freely
allow an unchanging current but opposes a rapidly changing one.
Electric power

Electric power is the rate at which electric energy is transferred by an <color=#3366CC>electric circuit</color>. The <color=#3366CC>SI</color> unit of <color=#3366CC>power</color> is the <color=#3366CC>watt</color>,
one <color=#3366CC>joule</color> per <color=#3366CC>second</color>.
Electric power, like <color=#3366CC>mechanical power</color>, is the rate of doing work, measured in <color=#3366CC>watts</color>, and represented by the letter P.
The term wattage is used colloquially to mean "electric power in watts." The electric power in watts produced by an
electric current I consisting of a charge of Q coulombs every t seconds passing through an <color=#3366CC>electric potential</color> (<color=#3366CC>voltage</color>)
difference of V is where Q is electric charge in <color=#3366CC>coulombs</color> t is time in seconds I is electric current in <color=#3366CC>amperes</color> V is electric
potential or voltage in <color=#3366CC>volts</color>
Electric power is generally supplied to businesses and homes by the electric power industry. Electricity is usually sold
by the <color=#3366CC>kilowatt hour</color> (3.6 MJ) which is the product of power in kilowatts multiplied by running time in hours. Electric
utilities measure power using electricity meters, which keep a running total of the electric energy delivered to a
customer. Unlike <color=#3366CC>fossil fuels</color>, electricity is a low <color=#3366CC>entropy</color> form of energy and can be converted into motion or many other
forms of energy with high efficiency.
Electronics
Electronics deals with <color=#3366CC>electrical circuits</color> that involve active electrical components such as <color=#3366CC>vacuum tubes</color>, <color=#3366CC>transistors</color>,
<color=#3366CC>diodes</color>, <color=#3366CC>sensors</color> and <color=#3366CC>integrated circuits</color>, and associated passive interconnection technologies. The nonlinear behaviour
of active components and their ability to control electron flows makes digital <color=#3366CC>switching</color> possible, and electronics is
widely used in information processing, <color=#3366CC>telecommunications</color>, and <color=#3366CC>signal processing</color>. Interconnection technologies such
as <color=#3366CC>circuit boards</color>, electronics packaging technology, and other varied forms of communication infrastructure complete
circuit functionality and transform the mixed components into a regular working <color=#3366CC>system</color>.
Today, most electronic devices use <color=#3366CC>semiconductor</color> components to perform electron control. The underlying principles
that explain how semiconductors work are studied in <color=#3366CC>solid state physics</color>, whereas the design and construction of
<color=#3366CC>electronic circuits</color> to solve practical problems are part of <color=#3366CC>electronics engineering</color>.
Electronic devices make use of the <color=#3366CC>transistor</color>, perhaps one of the most important inventions of the twentieth century,
and a fundamental building block of all modern circuitry. A modern <color=#3366CC>integrated circuit</color> may contain many billions of
miniaturised transistors in a region only a few centimetres square.
Electromagnetic wave
Faraday's and Ampère's work showed that a time-varying magnetic field created an electric field, and a time-varying
electric field created a magnetic field. Thus, when either field is changing in time, a field of the other is always induced.
These variations are an <color=#3366CC>electromagnetic wave</color>. Electromagnetic waves were analysed theoretically by <color=#3366CC>James Clerk</color>
<color=#3366CC>Maxwell</color> in 1864. Maxwell developed a set of equations that could unambiguously describe the interrelationship
between electric field, magnetic field, electric charge, and electric current. He could moreover prove that in a vacuum
such a wave would travel at the <color=#3366CC>speed of light</color>, and thus light itself was a form of electromagnetic radiation. <color=#3366CC>Maxwell's</color>
<color=#3366CC>equations</color>, which unify light, fields, and charge are one of the great milestones of theoretical physics.
The work of many researchers enabled the use of electronics to convert signals into <color=#3366CC>high frequency</color> oscillating currents
and, via suitably shaped conductors, electricity permits the transmission and reception of these signals via radio waves
over very long distances.
Production, storage and uses
Generation and transmission
In the 6th century BC the Greek philosopher <color=#3366CC>Thales of Miletus</color> experimented with amber rods: these were the first
studies into the production of electricity. While this method, now known as the triboelectric effect, can lift light objects
and generate sparks, it is extremely inefficient. It was not until the invention of the voltaic pile in the eighteenth century
that a viable source of electricity became available. The voltaic pile, and its modern descendant, the <color=#3366CC>electrical battery</color>,
store energy chemically and make it available on demand in the form of electricity.
Electrical power is usually generated by electro-mechanical <color=#3366CC>generators</color>. These can be driven by <color=#3366CC>steam</color> produced from
<color=#3366CC>fossil fuel</color> combustion or the heat released from nuclear reactions, but also more directly from the <color=#3366CC>kinetic energy</color> of wind
or flowing water. The <color=#3366CC>steam turbine</color> invented by <color=#3366CC>Sir Charles Parsons</color> in 1884 is still used to convert the thermal energy
of steam into a rotary motion that can be used by electro-mechanical generators. Such generators bear no
resemblance to Faraday's homopolar disc generator of 1831, but they still rely on his electromagnetic principle that a
conductor linking a changing magnetic field induces a potential difference across its ends. Electricity generated by <color=#3366CC>solar</color>
<color=#3366CC>panels</color> rely on a different mechanism: <color=#3366CC>solar radiation</color> is converted directly into electricity using the photovoltaic effect.
Demand for electricity grows with great rapidity as a nation modernises and its economy develops. The United States
showed a 12% increase in demand during each year of the first three decades of the twentieth century, a rate of growth
that is now being experienced by emerging economies such as those of India or China.
Environmental concerns with electricity generation, in particular the contribution of fossil fuel burning to <color=#3366CC>climate change</color>,
have led to an increased focus on generation from <color=#3366CC>renewable sources</color>. In the power sector, <color=#3366CC>wind</color> and <color=#3366CC>solar</color> have
become cost-effective, speeding up an energy transition away from fossil fuels.
Transmission and storage
The invention in the late nineteenth century of the <color=#3366CC>transformer</color> meant that electrical power could be transmitted more
efficiently at a higher voltage but lower current. Efficient <color=#3366CC>electrical transmission</color> meant in turn that electricity could be
generated at centralised <color=#3366CC>power stations</color>, where it benefited from <color=#3366CC>economies of scale</color>, and then be despatched relatively
long distances to where it was needed.
Normally, demand for electricity must match the supply, as storage of electricity is difficult. A certain amount of
generation must always be held in reserve to cushion an electrical grid against inevitable disturbances and losses. With
increasing levels of <color=#3366CC>variable renewable energy</color> (wind and solar energy) in the grid, it has become more challenging to
match supply and demand. Storage plays an increasing role in bridging that gap. There are four types of energy
storage technologies, each in varying states of technology readiness: <color=#3366CC>batteries</color> (electrochemical storage), chemical
storage such as <color=#3366CC>hydrogen</color>, thermal or mechanical (such as <color=#3366CC>pumped hydropower</color>).
Applications
Electricity is a very convenient way to transfer energy, and it has been adapted to a huge, and growing, number of
uses. The invention of a practical <color=#3366CC>incandescent light bulb</color> in the 1870s led to <color=#3366CC>lighting</color> becoming one of the first publicly
available applications of electrical power. Although electrification brought with it its own dangers, replacing the naked
flames of gas lighting greatly reduced fire hazards within homes and factories. Public utilities were set up in many cities
targeting the burgeoning market for electrical lighting. In the late 20th century and in modern times, the trend has
started to flow in the direction of deregulation in the electrical power sector.
The resistive <color=#3366CC>Joule heating</color> effect employed in filament light bulbs also sees more direct use in electric heating. While
this is versatile and controllable, it can be seen as wasteful, since most electrical generation has already required the
production of heat at a power station. A number of countries, such as Denmark, have issued legislation restricting or
banning the use of resistive electric heating in new buildings. Electricity is however still a highly practical energy source
for heating and <color=#3366CC>refrigeration</color>, with <color=#3366CC>air conditioning</color>/<color=#3366CC>heat pumps</color> representing a growing sector for electricity demand for
heating and cooling, the effects of which electricity utilities are increasingly obliged to accommodate. Electrification is
expected to play a major role in the <color=#3366CC>decarbonisation</color> of sectors that rely on direct fossil fuel burning, such as transport
(using <color=#3366CC>electric vehicles</color>) and heating (using <color=#3366CC>heat pumps</color>).
The effects of electromagnetism are most visibly employed in the <color=#3366CC>electric motor</color>, which provides a clean and efficient
means of motive power. A stationary motor such as a <color=#3366CC>winch</color> is easily provided with a supply of power, but a motor that
moves with its application, such as an <color=#3366CC>electric vehicle</color>, is obliged to either carry along a power source such as a battery
or to collect current from a sliding contact such as a pantograph. Electrically powered vehicles are used in public
transportation, such as electric buses and trains, and <color=#3366CC>electric cars</color>.
Electricity is used within <color=#3366CC>telecommunications</color>, and <color=#3366CC>electrical telegraphs</color>. With the construction of transcontinental, and
transatlantic telegraph systems in the 1860s, electricity had enabled communications in minutes across the globe.
Electricity and the natural world
Physiological effects
A voltage applied to a human body causes an electric current through the tissues, and although the relationship is
non-linear, the greater the voltage, the greater the current. The threshold for perception varies with the supply
frequency and with the path of the current, but is about 0.1 mA to 1 mA for mains-frequency electricity, though a current
as low as a microamp can be detected as an electrovibration effect under certain conditions. If the current is sufficiently
high, it will cause muscle contraction, fibrillation of the heart, and <color=#3366CC>tissue burns</color>. The lack of any visible sign that a
conductor is electrified makes electricity a particular hazard. The pain caused by an electric shock can be intense,
leading electricity at times to be employed as a method of <color=#3366CC>torture</color>. Death caused by an electric shock—electrocution—is
still used for <color=#3366CC>judicial execution</color> in some US states, though its use had become very rare by the end of the 20th century.
Electrical phenomena in nature
Electricity is not a human invention, and may be observed in several forms in nature, notably <color=#3366CC>lightning</color>. Many
interactions familiar at the macroscopic level, such as <color=#3366CC>touch</color>, <color=#3366CC>friction</color> or <color=#3366CC>chemical bonding</color>, are due to interactions
between electric fields on the atomic scale. The <color=#3366CC>Earth's magnetic field</color> is due to the natural dynamo of circulating
currents in the planet's core. Certain crystals, such as <color=#3366CC>quartz</color>, or even <color=#3366CC>sugar</color>, generate a potential difference across
their faces when pressed. This phenomenon is known as <color=#3366CC>piezoelectricity</color>, from the <color=#3366CC>Greek</color> piezein, meaning to press,
and was discovered in 1880 by <color=#3366CC>Pierre</color> and Jacques Curie. The effect is reciprocal: when a piezoelectric material is
subjected to an electric field it changes size slightly.
Some organisms, such as <color=#3366CC>sharks</color>, are able to detect and respond to changes in electric fields, an ability known as
electroreception, while others, termed electrogenic, are able to generate voltages themselves to serve as a predatory
or defensive weapon; these are electric fish in different orders. The order <color=#3366CC>Gymnotiformes</color>, of which the best-known
example is the <color=#3366CC>electric eel</color>, detect or stun their prey via high voltages generated from modified muscle cells called
electrocytes. All animals transmit information along their cell membranes with voltage pulses called <color=#3366CC>action potentials</color>,
whose functions include communication by the nervous system between <color=#3366CC>neurons</color> and <color=#3366CC>muscles</color>. An electric shock
stimulates this system and causes muscles to contract. Action potentials are also responsible for coordinating activities
in certain plants.
Cultural perception
It is said that in the 1850s, British politician <color=#3366CC>William Ewart Gladstone</color> asked the scientist <color=#3366CC>Michael Faraday</color> why electricity
was valuable. Faraday answered, "One day sir, you may tax it." However, according to Snopes.com "the anecdote
should be considered apocryphal because it isn't mentioned in any accounts by Faraday or his contemporaries (letters,
newspapers, or biographies) and only popped up well after Faraday's death."
In the 19th and early 20th centuries, electricity was not part of the everyday life of many people, even in the
industrialised <color=#3366CC>Western world</color>. The <color=#3366CC>popular culture</color> of the time accordingly often depicted it as a mysterious,
quasi-magical force that can slay the living, revive the dead or otherwise bend the laws of nature. This attitude began
with the 1771 experiments of <color=#3366CC>Luigi Galvani</color> in which the legs of dead frogs were shown to twitch on application of
animal electricity. "Revitalization" or resuscitation of apparently dead or drowned persons was reported in the medical
literature shortly after Galvani's work. These results were known to <color=#3366CC>Mary Shelley</color> when she authored <color=#3366CC>Frankenstein</color>
(1819), although she does not name the method of revitalization of the monster. The revitalization of monsters with
electricity later became a stock theme in horror films.
As public familiarity with electricity as the lifeblood of the <color=#3366CC>Second Industrial Revolution</color> grew, its wielders were more
often cast in a positive light, such as the workers who "finger death at their gloves' end as they piece and repiece the
living wires" in <color=#3366CC>Rudyard Kipling</color>'s 1907 poem Sons of Martha. Electrically powered vehicles of every sort featured large
in adventure stories such as those of <color=#3366CC>Jules Verne</color> and the Tom Swift books. The masters of electricity, whether fictional
or real—including scientists such as <color=#3366CC>Thomas Edison</color>, Charles Steinmetz or <color=#3366CC>Nikola Tesla</color>—were popularly conceived of
as having wizard-like powers.
With electricity ceasing to be a novelty and becoming a necessity of everyday life in the later half of the 20th century, it
acquired particular attention by popular culture only when it stops flowing, an event that usually signals disaster. The
people who keep it flowing, such as the nameless hero of Jimmy Webb's song "Wichita Lineman" (1968), are still often
cast as heroic, wizard-like figures.
Ip Man
Ip Man (born Ip Kai-man; 1 October 1893 – 2 December 1972), also known as Yip Man, was a Chinese martial arts
grandmaster. He became a teacher of the martial art of <color=#3366CC>Wing Chun</color> when he was 20. He had several students who later
became martial arts masters in their own right, the most famous among them being <color=#3366CC>Bruce Lee</color>.
Early life
Ip Man was born as Ip Kai-man to Ip Oi-dor and Ng Shui as the third of his parents' four children. He grew up in a
wealthy family in <color=#3366CC>Foshan</color> (Fatshan), <color=#3366CC>Guangdong</color> (Kwangtung) and received a traditional Chinese education alongside
his elder brother Ip Kai-gak, elder sister Ip Wan-mei, and younger sister Ip Wan-hum.
Ip started learning <color=#3366CC>Wing Chun</color> from Chan Wah-shun when he was 9 or 13. Chan was 57 at the time, and Ip became
Chan's 16th and last student. Due to Chan's age, he was able to train Ip for only three years before suffering a mild
stroke in 1909 and retiring to his village. Ip learned most of his skills and techniques from Chan's second-most senior
student, Ng Chung-sok.
At the age of 16, with help from his relative, Leung Fut-ting, Ip moved to <color=#3366CC>Hong Kong</color> and attended school at St.
Stephen's College, by then a secondary school for wealthy families and foreigners living in Hong Kong. Six months
after moving to Hong Kong, a classmate of Ip's named Lai told him that a friend of Lai's father who was an expert in
<color=#3366CC>Kung Fu</color> techniques was living with them, and had offered to have a friendly sparring match with Ip.
At the time, Ip was undefeated so he eagerly accepted the challenge. He went to Lai's house on a Sunday afternoon
and, after exchanging brief pleasantries, challenged the man to a duel. The man was Leung Bik and he easily
overwhelmed Ip Man. Incredulous at the speed with which he had been countered, Ip requested a second duel and
was beaten again, just as soundly.
Discouraged by his defeat, Ip left without a word and afterwards was so depressed that he did not dare mention that he
knew Kung Fu. A week later, Lai told him that the man he had fought was asking after him. Ip replied that he was too
embarrassed to return, at which point Lai told him that Leung Bik had highly praised his Kung Fu techniques and that
he was the son of Leung Jan, who trained Ip's master, Chan Wah-shun. Ip proceeded to train with Leung Bik, until
Leung's death in 1911.
Ip returned to Foshan in 1916 when he was 24 and became a police officer there for the Nationalist government. He
taught Wing Chun to several of his subordinates, friends, and relatives, but did not officially run a martial arts school.
Noted students of this time were Lok Yiu, Chow Kwong-yue, Kwok Fu, Lun Kah, Chan Chi-sun, and Lui Ying. Chow
Kwong-yue was regarded as the most talented of Ip's Foshan students, but he devoted himself to trade and abandoned
the martial arts. Kwok Fu and Lun Kah began teaching and spreading the art of Wing Chun in the Foshan and
Guangdong region. Chan Chi-sun and Lui Ying moved to Hong Kong but neither accepted students.
Ip married Cheung Wing-sing and they had several children: sons Ip Chun and Ip Ching, and daughters Ip Nga-sum
and Ip Nga-wun.
During the <color=#3366CC>Second Sino-Japanese War</color>, Ip Man sided with <color=#3366CC>Kuomintang</color> during the conflict. What Ip Man did during the
war remains unclear. It is rumoured that he had joined the Central Bureau of Investigation and Statistics in its academy
in <color=#3366CC>Guizhou</color> in 1938, after which he would have returned to Foshan as an undercover intelligence officer. However, the
veracity of this has been disputed. It is believed Ip went to live with Kwok Fu during the war and only returned to
Foshan at the end of the war.
After the war, Ip Man served for a few years as captain of the Foshan police patrols. Ip found some time to train his
second son, Ip Ching, during the year 1949. At the end of 1949, after the <color=#3366CC>Chinese Communist Party</color> won the <color=#3366CC>Chinese</color>
<color=#3366CC>Civil War</color>, as Ip was a member of the Kuomintang, Ip, his wife and their elder daughter, Ip Nga-sum, left Foshan for
<color=#3366CC>Hong Kong</color>.
Life in Hong Kong
Ip, his wife Cheung, and their daughter arrived in Hong Kong through <color=#3366CC>Macau</color> in 1950. His wife and daughter later
returned to Foshan to retrieve their identity cards. Due to the closure of borders between China and Hong Kong in
1951, Ip and Cheung were separated for good, with Cheung remaining in Foshan until her death.
After having moved to Hong Kong, the 56-year-old Ip Man struggled with unemployment. Ip's only prior experience was
as a policeman in Foshan, but he was either unable or refused to join the Hong Kong Police Force. Ip's friends were
able to help him get a job at a restaurant, where he would make new associates via the Hong Kong Restaurant
Workers' Association. The association also had a club for martial artists, led by Leung Sheung, but Ip Man didn't want
others to know that he was a martial artist.
Ip is known to have been addicted to opium and, after moving to Hong Kong, he was able to buy it on the black market.
Opium was very expensive at the time, so Ip had to earn a steady income to smoke opium while supporting his family
in Foshan.
Ip began teaching Wing Chun in the early 1950s, to escape poverty and to allegedly feed his opium addiction. His
earliest students consisted mainly of "poor and uneducated" members of the Restaurant Workers' Association and
"restless and angry young men", who were attracted to Ip Man's charismatic personality and the prospect of getting
tougher in order to survive the dangerous environment of 1950s Hong Kong. Initially, Ip Man's teaching business was
poor in Hong Kong because Ip's students typically stayed for only a couple of months. He moved his school twice, first,
to Castle Peak Road in Sham Shui Po, and then to Lee Tat Street in Yau Ma Tei, to where only a few of his former
students followed and continued to train with him. One of the notable students was Grandmaster Chow Tze Chueng,
the teacher of Sifu Donald Mak. By then, some of his students had attained proficiency in Wing Chun and were able to
start their own schools. They went on and sparred with other martial artists to compare their skills, and their victories
helped to increase Ip's fame.
Around 1955, he had a mistress from <color=#3366CC>Shanghai</color>, who was referred to by his students simply as Shanghai Po. Ip and
this mistress had an extramarital son named Ip Siu-wah. In Foshan, his wife Cheung died of cancer in 1960. Ip never
formally introduced his mistress to his other sons, who eventually arrived in Hong Kong to reunite with him in 1962.
By the 1960s, Ip Man was becoming more famous in the Hong Kong community. This allowed him to attract wealthier
and better-educated people to become his students. In 1967, Ip and some of his students established the Ving Tsun
(Wing Chun) Athletic Association. The main purpose of the Ving Tsun Athletic Association was to help Ip tackle his
financial difficulties in Hong Kong, which was due to his regular use of <color=#3366CC>opium</color>. One of his former students, Duncan
Leung, claimed that Ip used tuition money to support his opium addiction. Ip's mistress died of cancer in 1968, and their
son later became a Wing Chun practitioner, as did his half-brothers.
Death and legacy
Ip died on 2 December 1972, in his unit at 149 Tung Choi Street in Hong Kong, from laryngeal cancer, only seven
months before the death of <color=#3366CC>Bruce Lee</color>, his most famous student. He was buried at Wo Hop Shek, Hong Kong.
Ip's notable students include <color=#3366CC>Bruce Lee</color>, Moy Yat, Chu Shong-tin, Lok Yiu, Wong Shun-leung, Jiu Wan, Ho Kam-ming,
Victor Kan, Lo Man-kam, William Cheung, Ip Ching, Ip Chun and Leung Ting. Ip wrote a history of Wing Chun. Many
artefacts of his life are on display in the Ip Man Museum on the Foshan Ancestral Temple grounds. Ip Man is portrayed
in many films based on his life.
In 2000, Ip was inducted into the Martial Arts History Museum Hall of Fame.

Age of Discovery
The Age of Discovery (c. 1418 – c. 1620), also known as the Age of Exploration, was part of the <color=#3366CC>early modern period</color>
and overlapped with the <color=#3366CC>Age of Sail</color>. It was a period from approximately the 15th to the 17th century, during which
seafarers from European countries explored, colonized, and conquered regions across the globe. The Age of Discovery
was a transformative period when previously isolated parts of the world became connected to form the world-system,
and laid the groundwork for <color=#3366CC>globalization</color>. The extensive overseas exploration, particularly the opening of maritime
routes to the East Indies and <color=#3366CC>European colonization of the Americas</color> by the <color=#3366CC>Portuguese</color> and <color=#3366CC>Spaniards</color>, later joined by

the <color=#3366CC>English</color>, <color=#3366CC>French</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Dutch</color>, spurred <color=#3366CC>international global trade</color>. The interconnected global economy of the 21st
century has its origins in the expansion of trade networks during this era. The exploration created European colonial
empires and marked an increased adoption of <color=#3366CC>colonialism</color> as a government policy in several European states. As such,
it is sometimes synonymous with the first wave of European colonization. This colonization reshaped power dynamics
causing geopolitical shifts in Europe and creating new centers of power beyond Europe.
Portuguese oceanic exploration began with maritime expeditions to the <color=#3366CC>Macaronesian</color> islands, including the <color=#3366CC>Canary</color>

<color=#3366CC>Islands</color>, as well as <color=#3366CC>Madeira</color> and the <color=#3366CC>Azores</color>. It continued with voyages along the coast of <color=#3366CC>West Africa</color> in 1434, and
culminated in the establishment of a sea route to India in 1498 by <color=#3366CC>Vasco da Gama</color>, which initiated Portugal's maritime
and commercial presence in <color=#3366CC>Kerala</color> and the <color=#3366CC>Indian Ocean</color>. Spain made the transatlantic <color=#3366CC>voyages of Christopher</color>
<color=#3366CC>Columbus</color> (1492–1504), which marked the beginning of colonization in the Americas, the <color=#3366CC>Magellan expedition</color>
(1519–1522), which opened a route from the Atlantic to the Pacific and, under <color=#3366CC>Juan Sebastián Elcano</color>, completed the
first circumnavigation of the globe. Spain also undertook other major early voyages, including the <color=#3366CC>conquest of Mexico</color>
(1519–1521), the <color=#3366CC>conquest of Peru</color> (1532–1533), and the <color=#3366CC>Manila galleon</color> trade route (1565–1815), which linked the
Americas and Asia across the Pacific. These Spanish expeditions significantly impacted European perceptions of the
world and eventually led to numerous naval expeditions across the Atlantic, Indian, and Pacific Oceans, and land
expeditions in the Americas, Asia, Africa, and Oceania that continued into the 19th century, followed by polar
exploration in the 20th century.
European exploration initiated the <color=#3366CC>Columbian exchange</color> between the <color=#3366CC>Old World</color> (Europe, Asia, and Africa) and <color=#3366CC>New</color>
<color=#3366CC>World</color> (Americas). This exchange involved the transfer of plants, animals, human populations (including <color=#3366CC>slaves</color>),
<color=#3366CC>communicable diseases</color>, and culture across the <color=#3366CC>Eastern</color> and <color=#3366CC>Western Hemispheres</color>. The Age of Discovery and
European exploration involved <color=#3366CC>mapping the world</color>, shaping a new worldview and facilitating contact with distant
civilizations. The continents drawn by European mapmakers developed from abstract "blobs" into the outlines more
recognizable to us. Simultaneously, the spread of new diseases, especially affecting American Indians, led to rapid
declines in some populations. The era saw widespread enslavement, exploitation and military conquest of <color=#3366CC>Indigenous</color>
<color=#3366CC>peoples</color>, concurrent with the growing economic influence and spread of <color=#3366CC>Western culture</color>, science, and technology
leading to a faster-than-exponential population growth world-wide.
Concept
Mayflower IIMayflower II, a replica of the 17th-century English <color=#3366CC>sailing ship</color> Mayflower which transported a group of
<color=#3366CC>Pilgrim families</color> from <color=#3366CC>England</color> to the <color=#3366CC>New World</color> in 1620
The concept of discovery has been scrutinized, critically highlighting the history of the core term of this <color=#3366CC>periodization</color>.
The term "age of discovery" is in historical literature and still commonly used. J. H. Parry, calling the period the Age of
Reconnaissance, argues that not only was the era one of European explorations, but it also produced the expansion of
geographical knowledge and <color=#3366CC>empirical science</color>: "It saw also the first major victories of empirical inquiry over authority,
the beginnings of that close association of science, technology, and everyday work which is an essential characteristic
of the modern western world." Anthony Pagden draws on the work of Edmundo O'Gorman for the statement that "For
all Europeans, the events of October 1492 constituted a 'discovery'. Something of which they had no prior knowledge
had suddenly presented itself to their gaze." O'Gorman argues that the physical encounter with new territories was less
important than the Europeans' effort to integrate this new knowledge into their worldview, what he calls "the invention of
America". Pagden examines the origins of the terms "discovery" and "invention". In English, "discovery" and its forms in
romance languages derive from "disco-operio, meaning to uncover, to reveal, to expose to the gaze", what was
revealed existed previously. Few Europeans during the period used the term "invention" for the European encounters,
with the exception of <color=#3366CC>Martin Waldseemüller</color>, whose map first used the term "America".
A central legal concept of the discovery doctrine, expounded by the <color=#3366CC>United States Supreme Court</color> in 1823, draws on
assertions of European powers' right to claim land during their explorations. The concept of "discovery" has been used
to enforce colonial claiming and discovery, but has been challenged by <color=#3366CC>Indigenous peoples</color> and researchers. Many
indigenous peoples have fundamentally challenged the concept of colonial claiming of "discovery" over their lands and
people, as forced and negating indigenous presence.
The period alternatively called the Age of Exploration, has been scrutinized through reflections on the <color=#3366CC>exploration</color>. Its
understanding and use, has been discussed as being framed and used for colonial ventures, discrimination and
exploitation, by combining it with concepts such as the frontier (as in Frontier Thesis) and <color=#3366CC>manifest destiny</color>, up to the
contemporary age of <color=#3366CC>space exploration</color>. Alternatively, the term contact, as in first contact, has been used to shed more
light on the age of discovery and colonialism, using the alternative names of Age of Contact or Contact Period,
discussing it as an "unfinished, diverse project".
Overview
The Portuguese began systematically exploring the Atlantic coast of Africa in 1418, under the sponsorship of <color=#3366CC>Prince</color>
<color=#3366CC>Henry the Navigator</color>. In 1488, <color=#3366CC>Bartolomeu Dias</color> reached the Indian Ocean by this route.
In 1492, the Catholic Monarchs of Spain funded <color=#3366CC>Genoese</color> mariner <color=#3366CC>Christopher Columbus</color>'s (Italian: Cristoforo Colombo)
plan to sail west to reach the Indies, by crossing the Atlantic. Columbus encountered a continent uncharted by
Europeans (though it had been explored and <color=#3366CC>temporarily colonized by the Norse</color> 500 years earlier). Later, it was called
America after <color=#3366CC>Amerigo Vespucci</color>, a trader working for <color=#3366CC>Portugal</color>. Portugal quickly claimed those lands under the terms of
the Treaty of Alcáçovas, but Castile was able to persuade the Pope, who was Castilian, to issue four papal bulls to
divide the world into two regions of exploration, where each kingdom had exclusive rights to claim newly discovered
lands. These were modified by the <color=#3366CC>Treaty of Tordesillas</color>, ratified by <color=#3366CC>Pope Julius II</color>.
In 1498, a Portuguese expedition commanded by <color=#3366CC>Vasco da Gama</color> reached India by sailing around Africa, opening up
direct trade with Asia. While other exploratory fleets were sent from Portugal to northern North America, Portuguese
India Armadas also extended this Eastern oceanic route, touching South America and opening a circuit from the New
World to Asia (starting in 1500 by <color=#3366CC>Pedro Álvares Cabral</color>), and explored islands in the South Atlantic and Southern
Indian Oceans. The Portuguese sailed further eastward, to the valuable <color=#3366CC>Spice Islands</color> in 1512, landing in China one
year later. <color=#3366CC>Japan was reached</color> by the Portuguese in 1543. In 1513, Spanish explorer <color=#3366CC>Vasco Núñez de Balboa</color> crossed
the <color=#3366CC>Isthmus of Panama</color> and reached the "other sea" from the New World. Thus, Europe first received news of the
eastern and western Pacific within a one-year span around 1512. East and west exploration overlapped in 1522, when
a Spanish expedition sailing westward, led by Portuguese navigator <color=#3366CC>Ferdinand Magellan</color> (and, after his death in what is
now the Philippines, by navigator <color=#3366CC>Juan Sebastián Elcano</color>), completed the first circumnavigation of the world. Spanish
conquistadors explored the interior of the Americas, and some of the South Pacific islands. Their main objective was to
disrupt Portuguese trade in the East.
From 1495, the French, English, and Dutch entered the race of exploration, after learning of Columbus' exploits,
defying the Iberian monopoly on maritime trade by searching for new routes. The first expedition was led by <color=#3366CC>John</color>
<color=#3366CC>Cabot</color> in 1497 to the north, in the service of England, followed by French expeditions to South America and later to
North America. Later expeditions went to the Pacific Ocean around South America, and eventually by following the
Portuguese around Africa, into the Indian Ocean; discovering Australia in 1606, New Zealand in 1642, and Hawaii in
1778. From the 1580s to the 1640s, Russians explored and conquered almost the whole of <color=#3366CC>Siberia</color>, and <color=#3366CC>claimed Alaska</color>
in the 1730s.
Background
Rise of European trade
After the <color=#3366CC>fall of the Western Roman Empire</color> largely severed the connection between Europe and lands further east,
Christian Europe was largely a backwater compared to the Muslim world, which conquered and incorporated large
territories in the Middle East and North Africa. The Christian <color=#3366CC>Crusades</color> to retake the <color=#3366CC>Holy Land</color> from the Muslims were
not a military success, but they did bring Europe into contact with the Middle East and the valuable goods
manufactured or traded there. From the 12th century, the European economy was transformed by the interconnecting
of river and sea trade routes.
Before the 12th century, an obstacle to trade east of the <color=#3366CC>Strait of Gibraltar</color>, which connected the Mediterranean to the
Atlantic Ocean, was Muslim control of territory, including the Iberian Peninsula, as well as the trade monopolies of
Christian city-states on the Italian Peninsula, especially <color=#3366CC>Venice</color> and <color=#3366CC>Genoa</color>. Economic growth of Iberia followed the
<color=#3366CC>Christian reconquest</color> of <color=#3366CC>Al-Andalus</color> in what is now southern Spain and the siege of Lisbon (1147 AD), in Portugal. The
decline of the <color=#3366CC>Fatimid Caliphate</color>'s naval strength, which started before the <color=#3366CC>First Crusade</color>, helped the maritime Italian
states, mainly Venice, Genoa and Pisa, dominate trade in the Eastern Mediterranean, with merchants there becoming
wealthy and politically influential. Further changing the mercantile situation in the eastern Mediterranean was the
waning of Christian <color=#3366CC>Byzantine</color> naval power following the death of Emperor <color=#3366CC>Manuel I Komnenos</color> in 1180, whose dynasty
had made notable treaties and concessions with Italian traders, permitting the use of Byzantine Christian ports. The
<color=#3366CC>Norman conquest of England</color>, in the late 11th century, allowed for peaceful trade on the <color=#3366CC>North Sea</color>. The <color=#3366CC>Hanseatic</color>
<color=#3366CC>League</color>, a confederation of merchant guilds and their towns in north Germany, along the North Sea and Baltic Sea, was
instrumental in the commercial development of the region. In the 12th century, the regions of <color=#3366CC>Flanders</color>, Hainault, and
Brabant produced the finest quality textiles in northwest Europe, which encouraged merchants from Genoa and Venice
to sail there from the Mediterranean, through the Strait of Gibraltar, and up the Atlantic coast. Nicolòzzo Spinola made
the first recorded direct voyage from Genoa to Flanders in 1277.
Technology: Ship design and the compass
Technological advancements that were important to the Age of Exploration were the adoption of the <color=#3366CC>magnetic compass</color>
and advances in ship design.
The compass was an addition to the ancient method of navigation based on sightings of the sun and stars. It was
invented during the Chinese <color=#3366CC>Han dynasty</color> and had been used for navigation in China by the 11th century. It was
adopted by Arab traders in the Indian Ocean. The compass spread to Europe by the late 12th or early 13th century.
Use of the compass for navigation in the Indian Ocean was first mentioned in 1232. The first mention of use of the
compass in Europe was in 1180. The Europeans used a "dry" compass, with a needle on a pivot. The compass card
was also a European invention.
The ships of the Age of Discovery post-dated the fusion of the northern European and Mediterranean shipbuilding
traditions. Prior to the late 13th/early 14th centuries, northern European ships were typically clinker built, with a single
mast setting a square sail and a centre-line hung on the with pintles and gudgeons. Their counterparts in the
Mediterranean were built with carvel hulls, had one or more masts (depending on size) which set lateen sails, and were
steered with quarter-rudders positioned on the side of the hull.
Trade, pilgrimage and war brought ships from each tradition into the other's region, ultimately leading to the copying of
features that were new to each. Over the early 14th century, square sails started to be used in the Mediterranean, with
the mainmast setting square rig and the mizzen carrying a lateen sail. In the first two decades of the 15th century this
arrangement was copied in northern Europe where, by the late 1430s, some ships were built with carvel hulls. The
result of this merging of traditions was the full-rigged ship, a carvel hull with a sternpost-hung pintle-and-gudgeon
rudder and three masts: the foremast and mainmast setting square sails and the mizzen a lateen sail. Alongside this
type of vessel, the <color=#3366CC>caravel</color> was used. This type was also carvel built with a sternpost-hung rudder but could be
completely lateen rigged or have some square sails.
Very few wrecks of Age of Discovery ships have been found and archaeologically investigated. More is known about
Roman and Greek ships of <color=#3366CC>classical antiquity</color> than those of this period. The caravel is particularly poorly understood,
despite the number of "replicas" that have been constructed. However, a particular set of hull construction
characteristics have been identified from wrecks of this time, referred to as Iberian Atlantic shipbuilding tradition. They
are found in the Molasses Reef wreck, Highbourne Cay wreck, the Red Bay wreck and some sites in European waters.
Early geographical knowledge and maps
The Periplus of the Erythraean Sea, a document from 40 to 60 AD, describes a newly discovered route through the
<color=#3366CC>Red Sea</color> to India, with descriptions of the markets in towns around the Red Sea, <color=#3366CC>Persian Gulf</color>, and Indian Ocean,
including along the east coast of Africa, which states "for beyond these places the unexplored ocean curves around
toward the west, and running along by the regions to the south of Aethiopia and Libya and Africa, it mingles with the
western sea (possible reference to the Atlantic Ocean)". European medieval knowledge about Asia beyond the reach of
the <color=#3366CC>Byzantine Empire</color> was sourced in partial reports, often obscured by legends, dating back from the conquests of
<color=#3366CC>Alexander the Great</color> and successors. Another source was the Radhanite Jewish trade networks of merchants
established as go-betweens between Europe and the Muslim world during the time of the <color=#3366CC>Crusader states</color>.
In 1154, the Arab geographer <color=#3366CC>Muhammad al-Idrisi</color> created a description of the world and a <color=#3366CC>world map</color>, the Tabula
Rogeriana, at the court of King <color=#3366CC>Roger II of Sicily</color>, but still Africa was only partially known to either Christians, Genoese
and Venetians, or the Arab seamen, and its southern extent was unknown. There were reports of great African <color=#3366CC>Sahara</color>,
but the knowledge was limited for the Europeans, to the Mediterranean coast and little else, since the Arab blockade of
North Africa precluded exploration inland. Knowledge about the Atlantic African coast was fragmented and derived
mainly from old Greek and Roman maps based on Carthaginian knowledge, including <color=#3366CC>Roman</color> exploration of
<color=#3366CC>Mauritania</color>. The Red Sea was barely known and only trade links with the <color=#3366CC>maritime republics</color>, Venice especially, fostered
the collection of accurate maritime knowledge. Indian Ocean trade routes were sailed by Arab traders.
By 1400, a Latin translation of <color=#3366CC>Ptolemy</color>'s <color=#3366CC>Geographia</color> reached Italy from Constantinople. The rediscovery of Roman
geographical knowledge was a revelation, both for map-making and worldview, although reinforcing the idea that the
Indian Ocean was landlocked.
Medieval European travel (1241–1438)
A prelude to the Age of Discovery was a series of European expeditions crossing <color=#3366CC>Eurasia</color> by land in the late Middle
Ages. The <color=#3366CC>Mongols</color> had threatened Europe, but Mongol states also unified much of Eurasia and, from 1206 on, the <color=#3366CC>Pax</color>
<color=#3366CC>Mongolica</color> allowed safe trade routes and communication lines from the Middle East to China. The close Italian links to
the <color=#3366CC>Levant</color> raised curiosity and commercial interest in countries which lay further east. There are a few accounts of
merchants from North Africa and the Mediterranean, who traded in the Indian Ocean in late medieval times (see also ).
Christian embassies were sent as far as <color=#3366CC>Karakorum</color> during the <color=#3366CC>Mongol invasions of the Levant</color>, from which they gained
a greater understanding of the world. The first of these travellers was <color=#3366CC>Giovanni da Pian del Carpine</color>, dispatched by
<color=#3366CC>Pope Innocent IV</color> to the Great Khan, who journeyed to <color=#3366CC>Mongolia</color> and back from 1241 to 1247. Russian prince Yaroslav
of Vladimir, and his sons <color=#3366CC>Alexander Nevsky</color> and Andrey II of Vladimir, travelled to the Mongolian capital. Though having
strong political implications, their journeys left no detailed accounts. Other travellers followed, like French André de
Longjumeau and Flemish <color=#3366CC>William of Rubruck</color>, who reached China through Central Asia. <color=#3366CC>Marco Polo</color>, a Venetian
merchant, dictated an account of journeys throughout Asia from 1271 to 1295, describing being a guest at the <color=#3366CC>Yuan</color>
<color=#3366CC>dynasty</color> court of <color=#3366CC>Kublai Khan</color> in <color=#3366CC>Travels</color>. It was read throughout Europe.
The Muslim fleet guarding the Strait of Gibraltar was defeated by Genoa in 1291. In that year, the Genoese attempted
their first Atlantic exploration when merchant brothers Vadino and Ugolino Vivaldi sailed from Genoa with two galleys,
but disappeared off the Moroccan coast, feeding fears of oceanic travel. From 1325 to 1354, a Moroccan scholar from
<color=#3366CC>Tangier</color>, <color=#3366CC>Ibn Battuta</color>, journeyed through North Africa, the Sahara desert, West Africa, Southern Europe, Eastern
Europe, the Horn of Africa, the Middle East, and Asia, having reached China. After returning, he dictated an account to
a scholar he met in Granada, The Rihla ("The Journey"), the unheralded source on his adventures. Between 1357 and
1371, a book of supposed travels compiled by John Mandeville acquired popularity. Despite the unreliable and often
fantastical nature of its accounts, it was used as a reference for the East, Egypt, and the Levant in general, asserting
the old belief that Jerusalem was the <color=#3366CC>centre of the world</color>. Following the period of Timurid relations with Europe, in 1439,
Niccolò de' Conti published an account of his travels as a Muslim merchant to India and Southeast Asia. In 1466–1472,
Russian merchant Afanasy Nikitin of <color=#3366CC>Tver</color> travelled to India, which he described in his book A Journey Beyond the
Three Seas.
These overland journeys had little immediate effect. The <color=#3366CC>Mongol Empire</color> collapsed almost as quickly as it formed and
soon the route to the east became more difficult and dangerous. The <color=#3366CC>Black Death</color> of the 14th century also blocked
travel and trade for a time.
Religion
Religion played a critical role in motivating European <color=#3366CC>expansionism</color>. In 1487, Portuguese envoys Pero da Covilhã and
Afonso de Paiva were sent on a covert mission to gather intelligence on a potential sea route to <color=#3366CC>India</color> and inquire about
<color=#3366CC>Prester John</color>, a Nestorian patriarch and king, believed to rule over parts of the subcontinent. Covilhã was warmly
received upon his arrival in Ethiopia, but forbidden from leaving.
During the Middle Ages, the spread of Christianity throughout Europe fueled the desire to sermonise in lands beyond.
This evangelical effort became a significant part of the military conquests of European powers, like <color=#3366CC>Portugal</color>, <color=#3366CC>Spain</color>, and
